The Twin Prime Conjecture. There are infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by exactly two. Examples include three and five, five and seven, eleven and thirteen, and twenty-nine and thirty-one. Such pairs are called twin primes. Despite its simplicity of statement, this conjecture remains one of the oldest and most tantalizing open problems in number theory, with no proof or disproof yet found. Two primes p and p plus two form a twin prime pair. Other examples include forty-one and forty-three, seventy-one and seventy-three, one hundred one and one hundred three. The conjecture claims infinitely many such pairs exist. Yet how many have actually been found is unclear for astronomically large ranges, despite extensive computational searches. Computational searches have verified the conjecture for primes up to incredibly large magnitudes, in the trillions, but this is not a mathematical proof. The conjecture is closely related to questions about prime gaps, the distances between consecutive primes, and how often small gaps occur. Proving or disproving the conjecture would have implications for the distribution of primes and may require deep insights into analytic number theory. The Twin Prime Conjecture asks about the overall density of primes and their frequent small gaps. Goldbach's Conjecture is another famous conjecture about additive properties of primes. The Infinitude of Primes asks whether infinitely many primes exist in general. This conjecture asks specifically about infinitely many dense pairs. Any resolution of the Twin Prime Conjecture may depend on advances toward the Riemann Hypothesis, which governs prime distribution in profound ways.
